title: Amendment 3: Increased Homestead Exemption; Lower Cap on Increases in Non-Homestead Property Assessments

context.text: Placed on the ballot by the Florida Legislature as CS/House Joint Resolution 1F during a June 1-3, 2026 special session called by Gov. Ron DeSantis; it passed the House 75-26 and the Senate 30-9 on June 2, 2026 (Florida Senate vote history). The Legislature changed the governor's proposal so it would not apply to school property taxes (Florida Phoenix). It needs 60 percent of the vote to pass. The Division of Elections database lists it as ballot number 3.

Ballot-language litigation: on August 3, 2026 a Leon County circuit judge ruled the Legislature's original ballot title and summary ("Save Our Homes from Excessive Property Taxes") "clearly and conclusively defective" and ordered the Attorney General to submit corrected language; the ruling did not remove the amendment from the ballot. The Attorney General released rewritten language on August 13. The Division of Elections database lists the amendment as active with the note "AG Letter (Title & Summary rewritten)" and shows the rewritten title and summary as its current text. No later court ruling on the rewritten language was found in the sources reviewed.

question.text: INCREASED HOMESTEAD EXEMPTION; LOWER CAP ON INCREASES IN NON-HOMESTEAD PROPERTY ASSESSMENTS. — This amendment increases the homestead exemption, for all non-school taxes, to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028, and adjusts for inflation thereafter. It requires the Legislature to prescribe a uniform procedure for counties and municipalities, for their respective levies, to increase the homestead exemption up to full assessed value, and allows special districts, subject to referendum approval, to do the same. Persons who are not Florida residents on December 31, 2026, will receive the existing homestead exemption upon qualifying for a homestead exemption, with the increased homestead exemption beginning with the fifth year of exemption, to the extent permitted by the U.S. Constitution. This amendment reduces the annual cap on assessment increases for non-homestead properties from 10% to 5%. This amendment requires counties and municipalities to use property taxes solely for public safety, education and schools, infrastructure, natural resources, bond debt service, retirement benefits for employees, and operations and administration. Other expenditures may be approved by county officers or county or municipal governing bodies unless prohibited by general law, notwithstanding Article VII, Section 9(a) of the Florida Constitution, which allows counties and municipalities to levy property taxes for their respective purposes. This amendment takes effect January 1, 2027.

summary.text: The amendment would raise the homestead exemption for non-school property taxes to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028, indexed to inflation afterward, leaving the existing $25,000 exemption for school taxes; require the Legislature to set a uniform procedure for counties and cities (and, with referendum approval, special districts) to raise the exemption up to full assessed value; give people who are not Florida residents on December 31, 2026 the existing exemption at first, with the larger exemption starting in the fifth year of exemption; cut the annual assessment-increase cap on non-homestead property from 10 percent to 5 percent; and limit counties' and municipalities' use of property taxes to listed purposes, with other spending allowed if approved by county officers or governing bodies and not prohibited by general law. Fiscal impact: the Legislature's Revenue Estimating Conference estimated the amendment would cut local property tax collections by about $11.8 billion in fiscal year 2031-32 (WTXL); supporters dispute the projection, arguing it overstates the consequences and underestimates local governments' ability to reduce spending.

measure.yesMeans: Increases the homestead exemption for non-school property taxes to $150,000 (2027) and $250,000 (2028), lowers the non-homestead assessment-increase cap from 10% to 5%, and restricts what counties and municipalities may spend property tax revenue on.
measure.noMeans: Leaves the homestead exemption, the 10% non-homestead assessment cap and local property-tax spending rules unchanged.

argumentsFor.text: Gov. Ron DeSantis, in the proclamation convening the special session, stated that "Florida voters deserve the right to decide at the ballot box in 2026 on whether they continue to pay rent to the government in perpetuity through taxes on their homesteaded property," and noted that local governments collected $32 billion in property taxes in 2019 and are projected to collect $83 billion by 2032.

Florida Chief Financial Officer Blaise Ingoglia, a prominent supporter, said during a June appearance: "The numbers work," and "The only people who are complaining about it are the people who actually have to cut back. We are on the side of the taxpayers here." The Florida Phoenix also reported that Republicans who backed the resolution "argued homeowners need relief from rising tax bills."

argumentsAgainst.text: Following the Legislature's vote, the Florida Policy Institute put out a statement saying the proposal doesn't represent a tax reduction but a tax shift. "One that will force local lawmakers to cut local services that families rely upon or increase other taxes and fees to make up for the missing revenue," Institute CEO Sadaf Knight said in the statement. "In either case, everyday Floridians ultimately pay the price for the massive loss in property tax revenue."

Common Cause Florida, which has joined the "Save Our Services" campaign against the amendment, said through Executive Director Amy Keith: "If it passes, it will blow such a hole in local community budgets that it is certain essential services will be cut and everyday Floridians will be left holding the bag. Costs and fees will increase for small businesses, renters, and homeowners on fixed incomes, and more power will be centralized in Tallahassee." WLRN reported that opponents also include local government officials and law enforcement groups.

researchNotes: The Division of Elections' Initiatives / Amendments / Revisions Database (constitutionalinitiatives.dos.fl.gov) lists exactly three proposed amendments with 2026 ballot numbers 1-3 (all legislative referrals), and the Flagler County Supervisor of Elections' 2026 General Election page also lists three; the Department of State reports that none of the citizen-initiative petitions qualified. Florida requires 60 percent of votes cast. Florida publishes no voter-pamphlet arguments, so arguments are attributed quotes from news reports or official statements. The question text is the title and summary shown in the Division of Elections database after the Attorney General's rewrite; the database's 'Reference' line (Article VII, Sections 4, 6, and 9, and Article XII) is not part of the summary text and the printed county sample-ballot formatting was not retrieved (county sample ballots were blocked), so the printed heading format is unconfirmed. The enrolled joint resolution still contains the earlier ballot statement that the court rejected. Both sides have campaigns (supporters include the governor and Florida Realtors per news reports; the "Save Our Services" coalition opposes). Knight's statement was made after the Legislature's vote and is a description of the proposal's effects; the Phoenix report is cited via its Orlando Weekly republication because floridaphoenix.com returned 403. The Phoenix's June report of the Legislature's school-tax change and vote counts are matched by the Florida Senate vote history.
